lead: This unit explains what software is, why it needs engineering discipline, and how teams organise work through process models. After it, you can classify software, describe SDLC phases, compare waterfall, incremental, spiral, agile and XP, and name common reasons projects fail.
about: The unit starts with what software is, its application domains, legacy systems and common myths (1.1). It then explains software engineering as a layered practice with general principles (1.2), and lays out the SDLC phases from initiation to maintenance (1.3). Next it builds the generic process framework, task sets, umbrella activities and process patterns (1.4), then compares waterfall, incremental, spiral and the Unified Process (1.5). Agile development, Scrum and Extreme Programming follow (1.6). A short advanced chapter ties these ideas to why projects fail (1.7).

chapters.idea: Software is not just code: it is programs, data and documents, and its type decides the engineering approach.
chapters.depth: Define software; contrast with hardware (manufactured vs developed, no wear-out but deterioration through change). Cover changing role and evolving nature: from custom code to product lines, SaaS, embedded and AI-enabled systems. Application domains: system software, application software, engineering/scientific, embedded, product-line/reuse, web/mobile, artificial intelligence, legacy. Define legacy software and why it is kept. Software myths: management, customer and practitioner; correct each in one line. Some syllabi call application domains 'software application domains' and include 'legacy software'. Keep one short note on similarities and differences with other engineering products.

figure.aria: A tree classifies software into system, application, engineering/scientific, embedded, product-line, web/mobile, AI and legacy categories.

chapters.example: A Chennai IT firm maintains 40 applications: 25 custom web apps for clients, 8 embedded firmware for meter makers, 5 reusable payment libraries, and 2 payroll systems that are 12 years old. Classify the 40 into application domains and identify the legacy systems. Then correct the myth 'adding more programmers will catch up a late project'. Answer: 25 application/web, 8 embedded, 5 product-line/reuse, 2 legacy; adding people late adds communication overhead and usually slows a late project.
chapters.trap: Writing 'software = program'. Software includes data and documents; legacy is business-critical old software, not simply old hardware.
chapters.leave: Process models to 1.4–1.6; detailed project management to Unit 6; testing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Software engineering is a layered discipline: quality focus at the base, then process, methods and tools.
chapters.depth: Software engineering as a layered technology: quality focus, process, methods, tools. Essence of practice: understand the problem, plan a solution, carry out the plan, examine the result. General principles: keep it simple, provide value, maintainability, separation of concerns, modularity, abstraction, anticipate change, build with quality, think before coding. Practice areas: communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment (brief; expanded in 1.3–1.4). Some syllabi call this 'software engineering practice and general principles'. Include a short note on professional ethics and why tools do not replace process.

figure.aria: A stack places tools on top, then methods, then process, with quality focus as the base layer.

chapters.example: A 6-person team uses Git and Jira (2 tools), code review checklists (1 method), a 2-week sprint process (1 process), and a target of at most 2 defects per KLOC (quality goal). Map each item to a layer. If the team buys 5 more tools but keeps no process, which layer is missing? Answer: tools = Git/Jira; methods = checklist; process = sprint; quality focus = defect target. Buying tools without process leaves the process layer weak; tools alone are not engineering.
chapters.trap: Calling a toolchain 'the software process'. Tools support a process; they do not define it.
chapters.leave: Generic process framework to 1.4; SDLC phases to 1.3; project planning to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The SDLC is the set of phases a software product passes through, from initiation to maintenance.
chapters.depth: Life cycle activities: project initiation (brief: charter, scope, objectives; details in Unit 6), requirements, design, construction, testing, deployment, maintenance. For each phase: purpose, main output, who is involved, entry/exit criteria in one line. Show that phases can overlap and iterate. Some syllabi call this 'software development life cycle and its phases' or 'life cycle activities'. Keep requirements as an overview only; techniques belong to Unit 2. Mention feasibility study as part of initiation and requirements; detailed elicitation in Unit 2. Practical considerations: phase effort changes with project type, documentation level and risk.

figure.aria: A flowchart runs from initiation through requirements, design, construction, testing, deployment and maintenance, with a dashed feedback edge from maintenance to requirements.

chapters.example: A college fee portal has total effort 200 person-days. Planned split: requirements 15%, design 20%, construction 40%, testing 20%, deployment 5%. Compute person-days per phase. After go-live, a fee-rule change needs maintenance; which phase is repeated? Answer: requirements 30, design 40, construction 80, testing 40, deployment 10 person-days. A post-go-live change sends work back to requirements, then design, construction and testing as needed; maintenance is not a single code edit only.
chapters.trap: Assuming testing starts only after all coding and that phases never repeat. In practice phases overlap and change causes rework.
chapters.leave: Requirements engineering to Unit 2; design and UML to Unit 3; testing techniques to Unit 4; charter and scheduling detail to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A generic process framework gives the common activities and umbrella tasks that every project adapts into a specific process model.
chapters.depth: Generic process framework: communication, planning, modeling, construction, deployment. Defining a framework activity: tasks, work products, quality checks. Task sets: choose tasks by project size and risk. Umbrella activities: SCM, quality assurance, technical reviews, risk management, measurement, documentation. Process patterns: name, context, problem, solution, consequences. Process assessment and improvement: brief CMMI-style maturity idea without dates or numbers. Prescriptive vs evolutionary models; concurrent model. Some syllabi call this 'generic view of process', 'process framework', 'process patterns'. Unified Process can be mentioned as iterative/incremental but its phases are detailed in 1.5.

figure.aria: A tree separates the five framework activities from the umbrella activities that run across them.

chapters.example: A team defines a task set for one release: communication 6 tasks, planning 5, modeling 8, construction 12, deployment 4. It adds 3 umbrella tasks: risk review, QA audit, SCM baseline. Compute the total tasks and the percentage in construction. Answer: framework tasks = 6+5+8+12+4 = 35; total with umbrella = 38; construction share = 12/38 ≈ 31.6%. Umbrella tasks are not a sixth phase; they run across the release.
chapters.trap: Counting umbrella activities as sequential phases. They cut across the framework activities.
chapters.leave: Concrete models to 1.5; agile to 1.6; detailed risk, SCM and measurement to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Waterfall, incremental and spiral models arrange the same SDLC phases with different feedback, delivery and risk handling.
chapters.depth: Waterfall: strict sequence, document-driven, good for stable requirements; problems: late feedback, change is costly. Incremental: deliver product in increments; each increment passes through phases; early working software. Evolutionary: prototyping and spiral. Spiral: repeated loops; each loop has objectives, risk analysis, engineering, evaluation; good for high risk. Unified Process as iterative/incremental with inception, elaboration, construction, transition. Compare when to use each. Some syllabi call these 'prescriptive process models', 'evolutionary process models', 'conventional process models'. Mention concurrent model only as a note; do not detail.

figure.aria: A timeline compares waterfall's single test at the end with incremental releases and repeated spiral loops.

chapters.example: A payroll system needs 4 increments. Each increment takes 3 weeks to build and 1 week to test. Waterfall builds all 12 weeks, then tests for 4 weeks. Incremental tests after each increment. Find the week the first tested increment is ready and the week final testing ends for both. Answer: incremental first tested increment ends week 4; incremental final test ends week 16 (build 1–3, test 4; build 5–7, test 8; build 9–11, test 12; build 13–15, test 16). Waterfall final test also ends week 16, but no working tested version before week 16. Spiral would add risk analysis in each loop.
chapters.trap: Saying spiral is only 'waterfall repeated'. Each spiral loop must include explicit risk analysis; without it, it is just iterative development.
chapters.leave: Agile values and XP/Scrum to 1.6; detailed UP workflows to Unit 2–3; risk management to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Agile development uses short, repeated increments and close customer contact; XP adds specific engineering practices.
chapters.depth: Agile manifesto values and principles: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change. Scrum: roles (product owner, Scrum master, team), artifacts (product backlog, sprint backlog, increment), events (sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, retrospective), sprint length 2–4 weeks. XP: planning game, small releases, metaphor, simple design, test-first/TDD, refactoring, pair programming, collective ownership, continuous integration, 40-hour week, on-site customer, coding standards. Conventional vs agile. Some syllabi call this 'agile process', 'Extreme Programming (XP) Process', 'Scrum'. Keep one line on scaling only if needed; leave out details.

figure.aria: A tree groups Scrum events and XP engineering practices under agile development.

chapters.example: A team has velocity 10 story points per 2-week sprint. Backlog: login 5, search 8, report 3, payment 13, help 2. It adopts XP pair programming and estimates a 20% capacity drop. How many 2-week sprints are needed for all features? Answer: total = 5+8+3+13+2 = 31 points. New velocity = 10 × 0.8 = 8 points per sprint. Sprints = ceil(31/8) = 4; 4 sprints give 32 points. Plan highest-value features first; do not promise all in 3 sprints.
chapters.trap: Thinking agile means no plan or no documentation. Agile plans every sprint and documents as needed; XP pair programming is continuous review, not two people typing the same line.
chapters.leave: Requirements elicitation to Unit 2; testing techniques to Unit 4; CI/CD pipelines and DevOps to Unit 5; team metrics to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Software projects fail mostly through people, process and requirement causes, not only technical bugs.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic. Causes: unclear or changing requirements, unrealistic deadlines, poor estimation, weak stakeholder involvement, scope creep, inadequate testing, technical debt, poor communication, skill gaps, risk neglect, silver-bullet thinking and management pressure. Separate symptom from root cause. Early warning signs: rising defect backlog, slipping milestones, unresolved decisions, overtime, unclear ownership. One short note on blame-free retrospectives. Keep this chapter short; do not repeat full risk management.

figure.aria: A tree groups failure causes into requirements, management and engineering branches.

chapters.example: A project has 8 developers, 1 tester, a 6-month deadline and 120 requirements. By month 4, 30 requirements have changed, testing starts in month 5, and 2 developers leave. Name three likely failure causes and one early warning sign. Answer: causes include changing requirements (30 of 120), weak testing capacity (1 tester for 8 developers) and skill/staff loss (2 developers). Early warning: testing starts only in month 5 with a large untested build; defect backlog or slipping milestones would show it earlier. Mitigation: freeze or re-baseline scope, add test capacity earlier, and re-plan with the remaining team.
chapters.trap: Blaming failure only on 'bad programmers'. Requirements, schedule and testing capacity are usually stronger causes.
chapters.leave: Risk management and RMMM to Unit 6; test planning to Unit 5; detailed metrics to Unit 6.

links: weak process shows up as failure
